summary: Defines a DHCP option that tells a client the order in which to consult name services, such as DNS or local files, when resolving hostnames and other information.

plainLanguage.summary: This DHCP option lists name services in the order a client should consult them. A client uses the list to build its name-resolution search order.

questions: how to set name resolution order with dhcp
how does dhcp set name service order
what does name service search order mean
subtitle: A DHCP option that gives clients an ordered list of name services to consult.

tldr.problem: DHCP could provide name-service configuration but did not provide a standard way to state the order in which clients should use services.
tldr.mechanism: Option 117 carries 16-bit DHCP option codes in preferred order, referring to options that identify name-service servers.
tldr.outcome: Clients use the option to build a name-resolution search list, with detailed interpretation left to each system.

today: RFC 2937 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Search Order Is Sent
sections.content:
DHCP passes configuration information to hosts. DHCP already had options for providing information about name services, but clients that use several services had their own conventions for deciding which to query first.

This RFC adds a way for the DHCP server to supply that preferred order, using existing options that identify name-service servers.
sections.plainLanguage: A computer may have several sources for looking up names. This option lets the DHCP server say which source to try first.

sections.title: Option 117 Format
sections.content:
The option code is 117, and its minimum length is 2 bytes. The value contains 16-bit, big-endian DHCP option codes in preferred order; earlier entries are more preferred.

Examples include code 6 for DNS, 41 for Network Information Servers, 44 for NetBIOS name servers, and 65 for NIS+. Code 0 tells the client to use local naming information.
sections.plainLanguage: The server sends a list of numbered services. The client tries them in order, with the first listed service preferred.

sections.title: How Clients Use the List
sections.content:
A DHCP client uses the option to create a search list for name resolution. It may receive services that it does not support or has not been configured to access. It may also receive a service whose server-address option was not supplied.

The client interprets the list in a system-specific manner; that behavior is outside the scope of the RFC. DHCP provides no authentication or security mechanisms, as noted in the DHCP specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The option provides the order, but each client decides how to apply it. A client may not use services it does not support.
